findings.claim: The Church of England, by contrast, voted to ordain women as priests in 1994 and as bishops in 2014. (Repeated in the closing Key Fact, in practice question 3's mark scheme, in knowledge check 3's answer option and in the matching check's right-hand card.)
findings.truth: General Synod voted to ordain women as priests in 1992 and the first 32 women were ordained in 1994. Synod voted for women bishops in 2014, but the first woman bishop, Libby Lane, was consecrated on 26 January 2015. The lesson should read 'ordained its first women priests in 1994 and its first woman bishop in 2015'.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia: Ordination of women in the Anglican Communion; Wikipedia: Libby Lane (consecrated York Minster, 26 January 2015)

findings.claim: Reform Judaism in Britain and America affirmed same-sex marriage in 1990 and has conducted such ceremonies since. (Repeated in the closing Key Fact and in knowledge check 4.)
findings.truth: The 1990 decision of the Central Conference of American Rabbis was to admit and ordain openly gay and lesbian rabbis. Same-sex officiation was sanctioned in 2000. Reform synagogues in Britain have registered same-sex marriages since 2014, after the Marriage (Same Sex Couples) Act.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia: Reform Judaism (CCAR 1990 clergy decision; same-sex marriage sanctioned by 2000)

findings.claim: In 2024, Pope Francis approved the blessing of same-sex couples in pastoral contexts
findings.truth: Fiducia supplicans was published on 18 December 2023.

findings.claim: the Prophet Muhammad's final sermon, delivered at Mecca (lesson 1); The Prophet Muhammad's final sermon at Mecca stated that no Arab is superior... (lesson 2)
findings.truth: The Farewell Sermon was delivered in the Uranah valley of Mount Arafat during the farewell pilgrimage, not in Mecca.

findings.claim: The mark scheme for Theme F explicitly rewards students who name the sub-tradition... (also in the exam tip: 'The mark scheme explicitly rewards students who name sub-traditions', and in the conclusion: 'are what the mark scheme rewards')
findings.truth: No board mark scheme lists sub-traditions or promises credit for naming them. This is an invented mark-scheme claim. The advice itself is sound, so it is restated as house advice without the fabricated attribution.
findings.evidence: spec 4.4/4.5 assessment sections; house rule on copyright distancing and fabricated examiner claims

findings.claim: 4-mark question: 'Give two contrasting religious beliefs about the status of women in religious leadership. Refer to two different religious traditions or sub-traditions in your answer.' The mark scheme's examples pair Catholic with Anglican and Orthodox with Reform Jewish. Lesson 3's 4-mark question carries no tradition rubric at all.
findings.truth: Spec 3.2.1.6 requires contrasting beliefs on the status of women in religion, the uses of wealth and freedom of religious expression 'with reference to the main religious tradition in Britain (Christianity) and one or more other religious traditions'. Two sub-traditions of one religion do not satisfy that. Both questions now carry the correct rubric.

findings.claim: Each lesson's sixth practice question is labelled '2 marks - State / Give' (lessons 1, 2 and 3).
findings.truth: AQA GCSE Religious Studies A sets one five-part question per theme in Component 2, of 1, 1, 4, 6 and 12 marks. There is no 2-mark part. Each question is re-tariffed to the 4-mark form, with the stem asking students to explain and develop two points and the mark scheme giving 1 mark for each point plus 1 for its development.

findings.claim: the Truth and Reconciliation Commission, co-chaired by Tutu
findings.truth: Desmond Tutu was the chairman of the Truth and Reconciliation Commission. Alex Boraine was his deputy chairperson, not a co-chair.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia: Truth and Reconciliation Commission (South Africa)

findings.claim: the 'option for the poor' in Catholic Social Teaching, developed in Gaudium et Spes (repeated in practice question 5's mark scheme)
findings.truth: The phrase 'option for the poor' comes from Pedro Arrupe's 1968 letter to Latin American Jesuits and the Medellin conference of Latin American bishops in the same year, later developed by Gustavo Gutierrez and at Puebla in 1979. Gaudium et Spes (1965) laid groundwork but did not develop the option for the poor.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia: Preferential option for the poor

findings.claim: The Windrush Scandal, in which British citizens of Caribbean heritage were wrongly detained or deported from 2017 onwards
findings.truth: The wrongful detentions and deportations ran from the hostile-environment rules of October 2012 to 2017. Press reports began in November 2017 and the scandal broke as a political crisis in March-April 2018.

findings.claim: Mark-scheme answers name the specific argument and its grounding rather than stating a preference.
findings.truth: The 12-mark question requires a justified conclusion, and the lesson's own exam tip says the conclusion must state which side is stronger. Telling students not to state a preference would cost marks and contradicts the exam tip.
findings.evidence: spec assessment section (AO2 assessed through the 12-mark question); the lesson's own exam_tip_html

findings.claim: Examiners reward students who develop the link:
findings.truth: An invented examiner claim. The advice that follows is sound, so it is kept as house advice without the attribution to examiners.
findings.evidence: house rule on fabricated examiner claims

findings.claim: Practice question 3 is the 4-mark part but reads 'Explain two reasons why some religious believers support positive discrimination as a way of achieving racial equality.'
findings.truth: In Component 2 the 4-mark part is the contrasting-beliefs question, and the spec names only three issues on which contrasting beliefs are set for Theme F: the status of women in religion, the uses of wealth and freedom of religious expression. Positive discrimination is not one of them, so the paper would not set a 4-mark contrasting-beliefs question on it. Options: (a) leave the question as general 4-mark AO1 practice and add a line to the mark scheme saying the real 4-mark part is a contrasting-beliefs question on one of the three named issues; (b) rewrite it as a 6-mark 'explain two religious beliefs' item, which duplicates question 4; (c) leave untouched. Lesson 1 and lesson 3 now sit on named issues, so lesson 2 is the only one exposed.

findings.claim: Liberal Judaism has done so [ordained women rabbis] since 1975.
findings.truth: Jackie Tabick, ordained at Leo Baeck College in 1975, was Britain's first woman rabbi but served the Reform movement. Liberal Judaism's first woman rabbi is usually given as Julia Neuberger in 1977. I could not confirm a 1975 Liberal ordination, so I have not written a fix. Options: drop the clause, or change it to 'and Britain's first woman rabbi was ordained in 1975'.
findings.evidence: no source found that confirms a Liberal Judaism ordination in 1975

findings.claim: the Catechism of the Catholic Church (1994)
findings.truth: The Catechism was promulgated by Fidei Depositum on 11 October 1992; the English translation appeared in 1994 and the Latin editio typica in 1997. Both 1992 and 1994 appear in GCSE textbooks, so no marks are at risk.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia: Catechism of the Catholic Church

findings.claim: Strong sources include: ... the ummah (Islam) (also 'the ummah's teaching on human equality in Islam' in practice question 5's mark scheme)
findings.truth: The ummah is the worldwide Muslim community, not a source of wisdom and authority. Qur'an 49:13 ('We made you into nations and tribes so that you may know one another') is the source that carries the teaching. Left unedited because it would mean replacing long mark-scheme strings for no mark-scheme gain.
findings.evidence: Qur'an 49:13; the lesson's own glossary definition of ummah

findings.claim: The Quran states: 'And establish prayer and give zakat, and whatever good you put forward for yourselves - you will find it with Allah' (Quran 2:110, paraphrase).
findings.truth: The wording matches a standard translation of Qur'an 2:110 closely, so labelling it a paraphrase understates it. Students can quote it as a source.

findings.claim: The concept of the Jubilee year (Leviticus 25) - in which debts were cancelled and land returned to its original owners
findings.truth: Leviticus 25 restores land to its original owners and frees indentured Israelites; the seven-year release of debts is Deuteronomy 15. The pairing is standard in GCSE textbooks, so no marks are at risk.

findings.claim: Zakat is used throughout the lesson, the glossary and the practice questions.
findings.truth: The spec's key term is 'Zakah' (spec line 908). Zakat is a standard transliteration and would not be penalised, so this is a house-style note only.

summary: Three exam-form and six factual errors across all three lessons: every lesson carries a 2-mark practice question, a tariff AQA 8062 does not set (the theme question is 1, 1, 4, 6 and 12 marks); the 4-mark contrasting-beliefs rubric let students contrast two sub-traditions of one religion; and four passages claim the mark scheme or examiners reward particular techniques. The factual errors are Church of England women bishops (2014 for 2015), the Reform Jewish 1990 decision (gay and lesbian rabbis, not same-sex marriage), Fiducia supplicans (2024 for 2023), the Farewell Sermon (Mecca for Mount Arafat), the Truth and Reconciliation Commission chair, the option for the poor attributed to Gaudium et Spes, and Windrush dated from 2017. Scripture quotations, giving duties, charity founding dates and every knowledge-check answer key were otherwise correct.
